concepts.name: Salt as a Political Symbol: Strategic Choice by Gandhi
key_dimensions: Why salt was chosen over other grievances — universality across class, caste, and region
Economic burden of Salt Tax on the poor and its colonial justification
Comparison with other potential symbols (land revenue, textile boycott) and why salt was superior strategically
UPSC trap: distinguishing between the symbolic vs. economic rationale — both are correct but examiners test nuance

concepts.name: Gandhi's Letter to Viceroy Irwin (March 2, 1930): Ultimatum and Its Significance
key_dimensions: Content of the letter — 11 demands including abolition of salt tax, reduction of land revenue, military expenditure cuts
Constitutional and moral framing: Gandhi's use of nonviolent ultimatum as a political tool
Irwin's dismissive response and how it legitimized the march in public perception
UPSC trap: candidates confuse this letter with the later Gandhi-Irwin Pact correspondence — these are distinct events

concepts.name: The 11 Demands: Scope and Limitations of the CDM Agenda
key_dimensions: Full list of demands — salt tax, 50% cut in military expenditure, rupee-sterling ratio, total prohibition, release of political prisoners
Why the demands were deliberately moderate and not a direct call for Purna Swaraj
Tension between Congress's Lahore Resolution (Purna Swaraj, 1929) and the limited demands of the march
UPSC trap: conflating the Lahore Resolution's goal with CDM's stated demands — they differ in directness

concepts.name: The Dandi March: Route, Participants, and Organizational Features
key_dimensions: Date (March 12, 1930), starting point (Sabarmati Ashram), endpoint (Dandi, Navsari district, Gujarat), distance (~385 km, 24 days)
Composition of the 78 chosen marchers — deliberate inclusion of representatives from different regions and communities
Deliberate exclusion of women from the initial march and Gandhi's reasoning — later reversed as women became central actors
UPSC trap: the date Gandhi broke the salt law at Dandi is April 6, 1930 — not March 12 (the start date); frequently confused

concepts.name: Parallel Salt Satyagrahas: Geographic Spread of the Movement
key_dimensions: Simultaneous salt law violations across India — C. Rajagopalachari's Vedaranyam March in Tamil Nadu, Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan in NWFP
Significance of geographic spread in converting a Gujarat-centric event into a national movement
Role of regional leaders in adapting the salt satyagraha to local contexts
UPSC trap: questions often ask which leader led which parallel march — Vedaranyam (Rajaji) and Dharasana (Sarojini Naidu/Abbas Tyabji) are commonly tested

concepts.name: Dharasana Salt Works Raid: Nonviolent Resistance and International Optics
key_dimensions: Context: Gandhi's arrest on May 5, 1930 and the subsequent raid led by Abbas Tyabji, then Sarojini Naidu
Webb Miller's eyewitness report published globally — turning point in international perception of British colonialism
Significance as a demonstration of nonviolent discipline under brutal repression
UPSC trap: confusing Dharasana (post-arrest satyagraha) with the original Dandi March — they are sequential but distinct events

concepts.name: Role of Women in the Civil Disobedience Movement
key_dimensions: Shift from domestic roles to public activism — picketing liquor shops, foreign cloth shops, participation in salt satyagraha
Key figures: Sarojini Naidu (led Dharasana raid), Kamala Nehru, Kasturba Gandhi
Gandhi's evolving position on women's participation — initial exclusion from Dandi March, later active encouragement
UPSC trap: CDM saw greater women's participation than Non-Cooperation Movement (NCM) — this comparative point is frequently tested

concepts.name: Response of Different Social Groups: Peasants, Business Classes, and Minorities
key_dimensions: Indian business class (especially Marwari merchants) providing financial support — contrast with their lukewarm support during NCM
Peasant participation and limitations — uneven response, particularly where zamindari interests complicated the picture
Muslim participation: uneven — Ali Brothers had parted ways; Muslim League stayed largely aloof; some local participation
UPSC trap: generalizing that all minorities were absent — there was significant participation in specific regions like NWFP under Khudai Khidmatgars

concepts.name: Khudai Khidmatgar Movement (Red Shirts) and NWFP's Role in CDM
key_dimensions: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan's organization — significance of a nonviolent mass movement among Pashtuns (challenging colonial stereotype)
Integration of Khudai Khidmatgar into the broader Congress-led CDM
British response: particularly brutal suppression in NWFP — Peshawar incidents, Garhwal Rifle soldiers refusing to fire on crowds
UPSC trap: Frontier Gandhi is Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, not to be confused with other regional Gandhian figures

concepts.name: Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 5, 1931): Terms, Significance, and Criticism
key_dimensions: Key terms: suspension of CDM, release of political prisoners (not those convicted of violence), right to make salt for personal use on the coast, withdrawal of emergency ordinances
What the Pact did NOT achieve: no repeal of salt tax entirely, no inquiry into police brutalities, no reprieve for Bhagat Singh
Gandhi's defense of the Pact vs. criticism from socialists, youth leaders (Nehru's private reservations), and revolutionaries
UPSC trap: the Pact suspended CDM — it did not end it permanently; CDM was relaunched in January 1932

concepts.name: Second Round Table Conference (1931): Gandhi as Sole Congress Representative
key_dimensions: Context: Gandhi attended as the sole representative of Congress following the Gandhi-Irwin Pact
Failure of the conference — communal award deadlock, British unwillingness to concede dominion status or independence
Ambedkar's presence and clash with Gandhi over separate electorates for depressed classes
UPSC trap: Gandhi attended the Second RTC, not the First (1930) — Congress boycotted the first; this is a classic exam trap

concepts.name: Relaunching of CDM (January 1932) and Its Comparative Weakness
key_dimensions: Trigger: Irwin replaced by Willingdon; hardline policy — Gandhi arrested within hours of return, mass ordinances
Reasons for weakening: organizational exhaustion, business class withdrawal of support, Muslim non-participation, internal Congress divisions
Gradual withdrawal and formal suspension (May 1933, Gandhi's personal satyagraha withdrawal; 1934 formal end)
UPSC trap: CDM had two phases — 1930–31 and 1932–34 — confusing the timeline is a common error

concepts.name: Salt Laws and Colonial Economic Policy: The Legislative Architecture
key_dimensions: Salt Act of 1882 — legal basis for the British salt monopoly and prohibition on private salt manufacture
Revenue significance: salt tax as a percentage of colonial government income and its regressive nature
Historical continuity — Mughal salt taxation vs. British systematization of the monopoly
UPSC trap: the Salt Act violated in 1930 was the Salt Act of 1882, not a newer legislation — specificity matters in Prelims

concepts.name: CDM vs. Non-Cooperation Movement: Comparative Analysis
key_dimensions: Similarities: mass participation, nonviolence, Gandhi's leadership, use of hartals and boycotts
Key differences: CDM had a specific, tangible law to break (salt law) giving it focus; NCM was withdrawn abruptly after Chauri Chaura; CDM had greater women's participation and business class support
Organizational difference: CDM was more decentralized, allowing continuation even after Gandhi's arrest
UPSC trap: CDM is often called more mature/disciplined than NCM — but UPSC tests whether candidates know WHY, not just THAT

concepts.name: British Colonial Response: Repression, Ordinances, and Political Miscalculation
key_dimensions: Initially dismissive response ('Gandhi is making a nine days' wonder'), followed by mass arrests of over 60,000 participants
Emergency ordinances under Section 144, press censorship, suspension of civil liberties
Willingdon's hardline approach after 1931 vs. Irwin's relative pragmatism — policy shift and its consequences
UPSC trap: it was Irwin who signed the Pact with Gandhi, not Willingdon — viceroys and their policies are frequently mixed up

concepts.name: International Dimension: Global Impact and Media Coverage of CDM
key_dimensions: Webb Miller's dispatch from Dharasana reaching American and European newspapers — first major instance of Indian freedom struggle generating sustained global sympathy
American interest: parallels drawn with American colonial resistance to British taxation (Boston Tea Party analogy)
Impact on British public opinion and Labour Party's position on Indian self-governance
UPSC trap: global impact of CDM is underweighted in standard preparation — questions on this dimension appear in Mains Essay and GS1

concepts.name: Gandhi's Concept of Satyagraha as Applied in CDM: Theory vs. Practice
key_dimensions: Distinction between passive resistance and satyagraha — satyagraha requires active moral courage, not mere non-action
Constructive programme alongside CDM — khadi, village industries, untouchability removal as inseparable from political resistance
Test of nonviolent discipline: how Gandhi managed provocations by police without the movement degenerating into violence
UPSC trap: Gandhi explicitly distinguished CDM from mere law-breaking — the moral dimension (accepting punishment) is constitutive of satyagraha, often ignored by test-takers

concepts.name: Congress's Organizational Evolution During CDM: Towards a Mass Party
key_dimensions: Jawaharlal Nehru as Congress President during the launch phase — his ideological tension with Gandhi over the limited demands
Formation of Congress Socialist Party (1934) in the aftermath of CDM — left wing crystallization
CDM as a rehearsal for future mass mobilization — organizational lessons applied in Quit India Movement (1942)
UPSC trap: the Congress Socialist Party was formed AFTER CDM ended (1934), not during it — sequence errors are common

concepts.name: Poona Pact (1932): Intersection of CDM and the Question of Depressed Classes
key_dimensions: Communal Award (August 1932) by Ramsay MacDonald — separate electorates for depressed classes; Gandhi's fast unto death in Yerawada Jail
Poona Pact (September 1932): Ambedkar's agreement — reserved seats within joint electorates instead of separate electorates
Significance: demonstrates how CDM period was simultaneously a moment of anti-colonial struggle AND internal social contestation
UPSC trap: the Poona Pact increased the number of reserved seats for depressed classes compared to the Communal Award — candidates often think it reduced rights, which is incorrect

concepts.name: Historiographical Debates on CDM: Nationalist, Subaltern, and Revisionist Readings
key_dimensions: Nationalist historiography (Bipan Chandra): CDM as a high point of mass nationalism and Gandhi's political genius
Subaltern Studies critique (Ranajit Guha, Shahid Amin): peasant and lower-class participation had autonomous motivations not reducible to Gandhian ideology
Revisionist/Cambridge School (Anil Seal, Gordon Johnson): CDM as elite manipulation of mass sentiment for bargaining with the British
UPSC trap: Mains questions increasingly ask for multi-perspective analysis — presenting only the nationalist view is penalized in higher-scoring answers
